She'd found a coaching forum this way last month, and tonight she found something better, a summary of research by Gabriele Wulf, who had studied how people learn movement. The line that stopped her was this: learners usually improve faster when told to focus on the effect of a movement, such as the target, rather than on their own body parts. She read it twice. Her entire drill plan was built on body parts. Wrists, ankles, toes, tragedies.

"Everybody back," she called, crossing the yard, and knelt to set a cone in front of Maya's partner. "New rule. Forget your wrist. Forget your ankle exists. When you pass, hit your teammate's hands." She held up her own hands, palms out. "Right here. That's the whole job. The ball goes to the hands, and however your foot wants to accomplish that is its own business."

Priya laughed and said, "Even my feet can figure out where hands are," which was more philosophy than Morgan expected from a fifth grader, but the drill restarted and something changed almost at once. Kelsey, freed from inspecting her own toe, watched Priya's hands and put the ball flat into them. Dillon's pass had actual pace on it. Maya started calling for the ball with her hands up, which the others began copying, a little target rising all over the backyard, and Morgan stood on the sideline feeling like she'd discovered fire, or at least a decent match.

She kept the wrist stuff, though. Twice, when Priya's passes sailed high, Morgan said quietly, "Still the hands, but let the ball come off the ground a little less," and once she saw a release that looked cleaner and thought, without saying anything, that the ankle was probably locked this time. That was the part she couldn't resolve, that the body-part words seemed to help once the target idea had taken hold, or maybe they only seemed to, and she had no way of knowing without another practice, and probably three after that. She wrote on the clipboard, try hands only next week, then underneath, or maybe both, ask around, and underlined nothing, which for her was enormous restraint.

"Same time Thursday," she told the girls as they collected cones, and Maya jogged back for one more pass, hands already up, shouting, "Hit these," from the edge of the yard.

The market opened at seven, and by nine Lea had explained interest rates to a woman selling honey, twice to a man behind the tomato baskets, and once, desperately, to a toddler who had stopped to stare at her. None of it had helped. At noon she was supposed to stand in the community tent and give a five-minute talk for the credit union's scholarship, the one her mother kept calling the difference between State and nowhere, and the prompt was printed on the card in her pocket: explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation. She understood it. She had read four articles and watched two lectures. But every time she opened her mouth the words came out in the wrong order, like furniture carried through a door that was too small.

"You're doing it again," said Ruth, who sold bread at the stall Lea had been hovering near for twenty minutes. "Pacing."

"I have to explain money to strangers in three hours."

"Then explain it to me." Ruth wiped flour off her hands. "I raised four kids through two recessions. I'll tell you if you sound like a person or a textbook."

Lea took a breath and tried. She said that when the central bank raises its rate, borrowing gets more expensive, so people take out fewer loans, so there's less money chasing goods, so prices stop climbing so fast. It came out flat, a list wearing a coat. Ruth shook her head slowly, the way she did when a loaf hadn't risen.

"It's not wrong," Ruth said. "It's just not alive. You're suturing two things together with a thread nobody can see. Make them see the thread."

Lea sat down on a crate. Somewhere behind her a man was shouting about peaches, and the whole market had the warm, alluvial smell of a river valley in August, soil and fruit and rain-dust. She thought about her grandfather, who lived for the market's coffee and would be here within the hour, and about the fight they'd had at his kitchen table last week, when she'd claimed, airily, that central banks had always aimed at some fixed inflation number. He had laughed at her. Then he had gotten out his laptop, typed with two fingers, and made her read the screen aloud: New Zealand was the first country to adopt formal inflation targeting, when its government and Reserve Bank agreed in March 1990 on a target range of 0 to 2 percent. Not ancient history. Not always. Someone, somewhere, had decided to try it, on purpose, the year she was born's opposite.

That was the thread, maybe. Not a law of nature but an invention, an artifice people had built because the older ways kept failing. If it was built, it could be explained the way you explain anything built: what problem it solved, how the parts worked.

"Grandpa," she said when he arrived at ten, holding his coffee. "If I say New Zealand started it, is that right?"

"First country to adopt formal inflation targeting," he said. "Government and Reserve Bank, March 1990, target range of 0 to 2 percent." He sipped. "You looked it up with me. You should remember it."

"I remember. I want to use it. Tell me if this sounds like anything."

She stood between the bread stall and the peach man and tried again, this time starting from the story. Imagine prices climbing and nobody in charge saying what success would even look like, she said, until New Zealand wrote down an actual number, zero to two percent, and made its central bank accountable to it. Then the tool: to get inflation down toward that number, the bank raises the rate it charges, borrowing costs more, loans shrink, spending cools, and prices stop rising so fast. Ruth was nodding. A woman buying sourdough had stopped to listen.

"It's like turning the tap," the woman offered. "Rates up, water down."

"Kind of, except the water is everyone's mortgages at once," Lea said, and heard herself laugh, and heard the small crowd laugh with her.

At noon she stood in the community tent with her hands only slightly shaking and gave the talk, New Zealand first, the number plain on a card she held up, then the chain from a higher rate to slower climbing prices, then the honest part she had decided not to cut: nobody knows exactly how long it takes, and the cooling hurts some people before it helps everyone. When she finished, a judge asked what she'd study. "Economics," she said, surprising herself with how sure it sounded.

Afterward Ruth pressed a loaf into her hands, still warm, and said, "You sawed the thread for us." Lea walked out past the peaches holding the bread against her chest like something earned.

The chain drill fell apart for the third time in a row, and Hannah crouched behind home plate with her clipboard against her knee, pretending to write something. Nine eleven-year-olds stood in the outfield grass waiting for her verdict, and the verdict she wanted to give was not the one she should give.

She had watched them for two weeks before the league asked her to run practices. Their weakness was specific and stubborn: a throw to a cutoff man on the move. The ball either sailed into the runner's path, which was dangerous, or died short, which was embarrassing. So she had built drills. Cone markers. A bucket of balls. A relay pattern where the second baseman sprinted sideways and the shortstop had to lead him, throwing not to where he was but to where he would be. Every time a throw went wrong she called it out. Flat, she said, or late, or that's at his heels. Every time a throw went right she called that too. Good. Perfect. Again.

By the middle of the second practice, the drill looked clean. Nine throws out of ten arrived on the money. She felt a pride she distrusted, because on Saturday, in the actual game, the same kids had thrown to nobody, to ghosts, to patches of grass where no cutoff man had ever been. She had stood at the fence gripping the chain link and wanting to beseech them through it, as if her voice could travel the ninety feet her instructions apparently couldn't.

On Tuesday she arrived early, before any of them, and sat in the dugout with her phone. She had typed something into the search bar the night before, a phrase she'd half remembered from a documentary about flight simulators, and now she read the results slowly, twice. One line stood out among the paragraphs of jargon. Guidance hypothesis. Feedback after every single attempt could make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helped retention. She read it a third time, then looked out at the empty diamond, the bases still pale from morning rain, and felt the idea rearrange something.

"What's that face," said Marcus, eleven years old and the team's loudest shortstop, dropping his bag on the bench beside her.

"It's called the guidance hypothesis," she said, locking the phone. "I read it this morning."

"Sounds like homework."

"It kind of is."

She did not tell him the rest, and she did not tell Coach Denny either, though he arrived ten minutes later with his thermos and his habit of standing just behind her shoulder. Denny had run the Saturday game from the fence, calling cutoffs for every ball put in play, and the kids had still fallen apart, and Hannah had spent the drive home trying not to think about whose voice they'd been listening to all season. Including hers.

So she changed the practice, and the change felt like a gamble. She put the cones out, set the drill running, and then made herself walk away. She stood by the backstop and kept her mouth shut. The first throw was flat. She let it go. The second died in the grass ten feet short, and Marcus's shoulders tightened as he waited for the word that always came, and no word came, and he threw again, and this time the ball angled ahead of the runner, into the space he was about to occupy. Hannah's fingers ached against the clipboard. It would be so easy to say good, to be the voice under the words, and she made herself stay parsimonious with her praise, one comment in five throws, then one in ten, saying nothing that wasn't worth their depending on.

The kids got louder. That was the strange part. Without her voice filling the gaps they began to fill them themselves, the shortstop holding up two fingers, the second baseman calling cutoff early, a skinny kid named Eli who never spoke asking for the ball twice. Their throws were worse than Tuesday's, noticeably worse, and Hannah had to sit on the fear that she was ruining them, that an aphorism she liked, let them feel it, was just a cover for doing nothing. She had been the one who made the drill look clean with her corrections. The clean was hers, not theirs.

Denny came and stood beside her at the backstop. He watched a throw skip past the cone, and she felt him draw breath.

"Don't," she said, before she could weigh it. Then, more carefully, because he was a volunteer and unpaid and had been doing this for nine years, "Just for this drill. Try it once."

He held his thermos with both hands and said nothing, which she chose to take as agreement, and she knew it was only half agreement, and she let that be uncertain. He had his reasons. She had hers. One of them would turn out to be right and the other wrong, or, more likely, both of them were holding a piece of something, and Saturday would decide nothing cleanly.

She had not told anyone on the field why this mattered so much to her, and she told no one now. Four years ago her own coach had corrected her swing on every pitch of every practice, a running commentary she could still hear when she closed her eyes, and the day he was absent, with a scout in the bleachers, she had stood at the plate and realized she could not feel her own hands. She had quit that spring and told everyone it was her knee. Her mother still believed it was her knee.

"Scrimmage," she called out, walking onto the grass. "Eli, you're playing short. Marcus, you're a runner, full speed, don't be polite." She set a ball on the tee, jogged to the backstop, and put the clipboard down on the bench. Denny stayed where he was, thermos in both hands, silent.

Marcus broke from first on contact. Eli drifted toward the line, and the left fielder scooped the ball, and for one long second, with the whole practice watching and nobody saying a word, Eli had to decide on his own where the runner would be. Hannah held her breath. His arm came through and the ball left his hand, cutting across the grass toward a spot of empty air.

The line outside Courtroom 4B began forming at eight, and by eight twenty Kevin had memorized the back of the man ahead of him: a gray suit, a sweat stripe between the shoulder blades, a folder held the way people hold something they are afraid to drop. Kevin had his own folder, and inside it was the sheet he had been studying for three days, a page of notes on heads of government and how they come to power and how they go. His interview for naturalization was at ten fifteen. If the officer asked him a question about civics and he got it wrong, he would come back another day, and another, and his mother had already taken the morning off work twice.

The man in the gray suit turned around. "You look like you're studying for the bar," he said.

"Citizenship." Kevin held up the folder as proof, though the folder proved nothing. "There's a civics part. They ask you questions."

The man nodded slowly, the way people nod at a delay announcement. "My wife did it in 2011. They asked her who signs bills into law. She said the president and froze. Then she said, 'Unless it's a veto,' and the officer laughed and passed her." He turned back around, and Kevin went back to his sheet, which was not really about the United States at all.

Here was his problem, and he knew it was a problem. His notes had wandered. He had started, sensibly, with the American arrangement: a president elected directly, serving a fixed term, removable only through impeachment, which was long and hard and almost never worked. Then he had started comparing, because comparing was how he actually understood things, and somewhere in the comparison his notes had drifted across the Atlantic. In Britain, he had written, the prime minister is not elected by the people at all; the party wins seats and the party leader becomes prime minister, and if the parliament turns on that leader, the government can fall between elections, without any trial, without any crime. Two systems, two logics. He could feel that there was something important in the difference, some idea about trust and time and how much power a voter actually hands over, but he could not yet say what it was, and the interview was in two hours.

"You're muttering," said a voice to his left.

A girl about his age stood there with a clear plastic bag, the kind they made you use instead of a purse, and inside it a paperback and a passport. She had been behind him the whole time, he realized, and he had been mouthing his notes like a man praying.

"Sorry. I'm trying to figure something out before ten fifteen."

"What's at ten fifteen?"

"Either my citizenship or my second attempt at it." He said it lightly, but his hands were not light; they had rolled the folder into a loose tube. She looked at the tube, then at him, and something in her expression made him unroll it flat against his leg.

"What's the thing you're figuring out?" she asked.

He hesitated, because explaining a half-idea is worse than explaining nothing, and then he explained it anyway: the president with his fixed years, the prime minister who can fall any Tuesday. She listened with her chin tipped slightly, the paperback untouched in its bag.

"France," she said.

"What about it?"

"France does both." She said it the way you point out a door someone has been pushing on. "They elect their president directly. The president appoints the prime minister. But the National Assembly, their parliament, can force the prime minister's government out. They pass a censure motion, and the government has to resign." She shrugged. "My dad's French. We argue about it every Christmas."

Kevin stood very still, and the line moved forward without him for a second, and the man in the gray suit glanced back. In his head the two columns of his notes were reorganizing themselves around this new middle column, this thing that was neither one system nor the other. The president chosen by the whole country; the prime minister chosen by the president; and the assembly able to pull the prime minister down anyway. It was not a compromise so much as an admission that two kinds of legitimacy could exist at once and fight inside a single government. He had been thinking of the systems as answers, and now he was thinking of them as arguments that never end.

"But wait," he said. "So who do the French actually hold accountable? If the government resigns, the president just picks someone else, right? The voter didn't pick the prime minister in the first place."

"That," the girl said, "is the Christmas argument. My dad says the voter is playing the long game. I say it's like being handed deterrence instead of control. You can't choose the government, but you can always threaten to take it down." She smiled slightly. "He says I've been reading too much American political science. I say he's axiomatic about parliamentary government. He thinks that's an insult. I looked it up; it isn't."

The line reached the doors. Inside, the hallway smelled of floor wax and old paper, and a marshal was telling people to have their documents ready, and Kevin realized the borders of the morning had quietly narrowed to a single corridor, a single desk, a single officer who would ask him something he could not fully predict. He would not be asked about France. He knew that. The civics questions delimitated a small and knowable country, and he knew that country well enough now. What France had given him was not on any test: it was the beginning of a considered position, that no system escapes the trade, that each one draws the line between stability and accountability somewhere, and that wherever it draws it, someone is standing outside it, muttering into a folder. He slid the sheet back in among his documents, unverified, untested, his.

"You'll pass," the girl said. She was three people behind him now, holding her passport up so the marshal could see the seal on it. "You clearly care more than anyone else in this line."

"Ten fifteen," Kevin said to the marshal, showing his appointment letter.

"Room C. Window two."

He walked down the corridor with the folder pressed flat under his arm, and behind him the girl called out, "Merry Christmas argument," and laughed.

Maria spread the photocopy across the piano lid and discovered, with a small groan, that she had left her pencil at home. The music room smelled of cork floor and valve oil, and outside the window the lacrosse team was running drills in the rain, which struck her as a heroic and stupid thing to be doing while she sat indoors arguing with Mozart.

The argument was this: her assignment sheet said the first movement of the sonata in question was in sonata form, with an exposition, a development, and a recapitulation, and her job was to draw lines in the score marking where each section began. She had listened to the recording twice on the bus and had a theory about the exposition, roughly bars one through fifty-six, give or take her own willingness to commit. The development, she suspected, began at the place where the music turned restless and started wandering through keys like someone checking every drawer in the house for keys that were already in her pocket.

"You look like a detective," said Priya from the doorway, shaking rain off her jacket. Priya had agreed to meet her here partly for the company and partly because the music room had the good radiator. "A detective who's lost."

"I'm fine," Maria said, with the dignity of someone who had just been mouthing bar numbers. "I need a pencil, and I need to know where the recapitulation starts, and I need it not to be bar ninety-three."

Priya dug through her bag and produced a pencil chewed at one end, a green felt-tip, and a broken crayon labelled "burnt sienna," offering all three with the flourish of a street vendor. Maria chose the felt-tip. It would look unhinged in the margin of an exam, but she was not thinking about the exam; she was thinking about the second theme, the slinking little tune that arrived around bar twenty and, in a detail she could not stop noticing, did not sound the same the second time she met it.

She set the metronome ticking, found the opening on the piano with two tentative fingers, and played until the second theme arrived. Then she hunted for its later twin. Priya, meanwhile, had installed herself at the radiator and begun to gesticulate along with the metronome like an increasingly ambitious orchestra conductor, which Maria tolerated because Priya's waving arms actually helped her keep count.

"There," Maria said, marking bar ninety-three, where the first theme came back in its original clothes. "Recapitulation." But when she followed the second theme to its return, she stopped, drew a small circle around the key signature, then another circle, then a rectangle of pure green outrage around both. "It moved."

"It moved where?"

"Listen." She played the second theme as it appeared in the exposition, then as it came back in the recapitulation, side by side, and Priya's conducting arms slowed, then dropped. The two versions were the same tune, the same shape, but the second one sat lower, at home, in the key the whole movement had started in. "In the exposition it's up in the dominant," Maria said, mostly to herself. "In the recapitulation it comes back in the home key. So the movement ends settled in the key where it began." She said it again, quieter, because it sounded like a rule someone had handed her, except nobody had; the score had.

Priya peered at the green carnage on the page. "So Mozart was just tidy?"

"No, it's, " Maria began, and then stopped, because she had been about to say it was a contrivance, a machine for leaving home and coming back, and the word felt both exactly right and slightly unfair, like calling a good plot a trick. "It's a contrivance," she said anyway, "but a good one. The whole first half builds the tension of two keys, and the second half resolves it." She hesitated. "Probably. That might be the tidy version. Maybe it's not about tension at all. I don't know what he wanted, and I don't think I'm supposed to pretend I do."

"You're very intransigent about a dead guy," Priya said, poking her in the arm. "He's not going to argue back."

"He's absolutely arguing back. Every time I draw a line he moves it." Maria drew the line anyway, after the development, before the recapitulation, and next to it wrote her one honest sentence in green: the second theme returns in the home key, not the dominant, so the movement ends settled in the key where it began. Then, underneath, smaller: but why it satisfies me, I can't say.

Priya leaned over and read it. "You know the exam won't grade the last part."

"The exam's the exam," Maria said. She gathered the pencil crayon and the chewed pencil back into Priya's bag, folded the score, and played the final bars once more, both hands, slow, listening to the music sitting down at last in its own front hallway.

"Same time Thursday?" said Priya, from the doorway.

"Bring two pencils," said Maria.

The printout of Texas v. Johnson was forty-six pages, and Claire had read it three times on the porch of her grandfather's house while the cicadas sawed away in the August heat. Her government teacher had assigned sides by lottery, and Claire had drawn the harder one: she would argue against the flag burner before the mock court in September, against her own instincts, against the ruling itself. The problem was that the ruling had won. She kept circling the top of the first page, where the vote was recorded, five to four, and she could not make those numbers feel like the settled law everyone pretended it was.

Her grandfather came out with two glasses of iced tea and set one beside her chair without asking whether she wanted it. He had flown helicopters in Vietnam for two tours, and a small flag hung from the porch rail where he raised it each morning and lowered it each dusk, folding it into a neat triangle with hands that did not hesitate.

"Still homework," he said. It wasn't a question.

"I have to argue that burning the flag should be illegal. In front of a panel of seniors playing the justices." She held up the printout. "The case is Texas v. Johnson. 1989. The Supreme Court ruled five to four that burning the flag as political protest is protected symbolic speech."

He sat down across from her and looked at the trees for a while. "Five to four," he said finally. "You know what that means."

"That it was close."

"That the best legal minds in the country split down the middle, and the side you're arguing had four of them on it."

She had known that, but hearing him say it rearranged something. All summer she had been treating the assignment as a losing cause, a exercise in defending the indefensible, and now she understood she had been treating the law itself the same way, as a wall when it was more like a door someone had pushed open by a single hand's width. The subtlety of it embarrassed her. She had wanted the case to be simple so that she could be simply right.

"Will you listen to me practice?" she asked.

"I'll do better than that." He set down his tea. "I'll argue the other side."

They started that evening at the kitchen table, her notes on one side, his folding chair pulled up opposite hers. She made her case first: the flag stands for something beyond any one speaker's message, it belongs to everyone, and destroying it to make a point appropriates a symbol that is jointly held. Her grandfather listened with his forearms on the table, then stood and delivered the rebuttal like a man who had been waiting thirty years for the chance. The government cannot decide which symbols are sacred, he said. That is exactly the power the First Amendment exists to prevent. He was better than she expected, and partway through she realized he was using her own phrasing back at her, from an editorial she'd written junior year, the one about school censorship of the student paper that he had clipped and mailed back to her with a sticky note saying "proud of this."

"Did you keep that?" she asked, when he finished.

"I keep everything you write." He said it flatly, and the kitchen went quiet except for the ice settling in the glasses.

They argued every evening for a week. Claire discovered that her strongest material came from the losing side's own dissent, the argument that the flag's unique position in American life underwrote a narrow exception to otherwise broad protections, that some symbols carry a meaning so widely shared that burning one is less like speech and more like a slap. She also discovered, reading deeper, that the majority had a point she could not shake: once the government may protect a symbol from insult, it may protect anything from insult, and the list of protected things would be written by whoever held power. She took both arguments to bed with her and lay awake under the fan, holding them the way you hold two stones of nearly equal weight, one in each hand.

The night before she left for the drive home, her grandfather lowered the flag at dusk while she watched from the steps. His hands went through the same sequence they always did, unhurried, precise, and she thought about what the ritual would mean to someone watching it as pure theater, someone who had never folded one over a coffin.

"You never told me what you actually think," she said. "Which side won, in your head."

He tucked the triangle under his arm and stood there in the fading light. "I think four justices were right, and I think the five had to win anyway." He looked at her. "I don't know how to say it better than that."

She had come wanting him to resolve it, she saw that now, wanting the veteran to hand her either permission or prohibition so the case would stop being double in her hands. He hadn't, and she found she was grateful, because on the drive home tomorrow she would be the only one standing in front of that panel, and whatever she argued would have to be hers, including the parts she still couldn't reconcile.

"Argue it like the vote hasn't happened yet," he said. "Argue like you're the fifth vote either way." He carried the folded flag up the steps past her, into the house, and hung it on the brass hook inside the door.

Simon's problem was not the sphygmomanometer, which he could wrap around an arm and inflate with reasonable dignity, but the number it produced. One hundred and sixty-eight over ninety-five, on Grandpa Lou's wrist, Tuesday night at the kitchen table, while the pot of chicken soup went on bubbling behind them as though nothing had happened.

The school's health elective had a certification test on Friday: take a reading, interpret it, and explain to the examiner how diet and exercise could change it. Miss Okafor had made them practice on each other all week, and Simon's partner, Priya, kept narrating like a nature documentary. "The wild cuff closes in on its prey," she'd said, squeezing the bulb. "Notice how the arteries atrophy from disuse, like the rest of us in gym." That was Priya's whole method: wrong facts delivered with total confidence, which Simon had stopped correcting around October because it was funnier that way.

The blood pressure unit had seemed abstract until Tuesday. Now there was a number attached to a man who salted his soup twice before tasting it, once out of habit and once, he claimed, "for luck."

Grandpa Lou's kitchen was an archive of cans. Wednesday evening Simon sat on the counter with his phone and a can of the soup itself, reading labels aloud like a courtroom clerk. One serving contained eight hundred ninety milligrams of sodium, and the can held two and a half servings. He did the math twice, because the first answer seemed like an accusation.

"Grandpa. The World Health Organization says adults should eat less than two grams of sodium a day for blood pressure. That's less than five grams of salt total." He held up the can. "This is most of it. This one can."

"That seems capricious," Grandpa said, stirring. "How can they set one number for everybody? Your grandmother ate salt like a sailor and lived to ninety."

"That's not a sample size, that's one person."

"One excellent person," Grandpa said, and Simon laughed despite himself, and then went quiet, because a person was exactly the problem. The textbook talked about populations, about averages across millions of hearts, and here was a single heart across the table, eighty-one years old, beating one hundred sixty-eight over ninety-five, loving a food that textbooks would call, if textbooks made jokes, a health food oxymoron. Simon's cupboards at home held his mother's flaxseed and Grandpa's salt shaker, two philosophies sharing one drawer.

He texted Priya that night, and her reply arrived like a ransom note: "test is FRIDAY 9am. you still sound like you think the textbook is a moral judgment. it's not, it's a weather report. you can argue with rain all you want but bring an umbrella." He read it three times. It was the most useful thing anyone had said to him all week, and he hated that slightly, because Priya hadn't even been trying.

Thursday he tried the other direction. He walked the loop behind the school with Grandpa Lou, who complained for the first quarter mile and then, somewhere past the tennis courts, stopped complaining and started telling a story about a girl he'd liked in 1962, and by the end of the mile he was slightly pink and breathing like a man who had done something. Simon took his blood pressure when they got back to the car: one fifty-eight over ninety. Better, but not fixed, and Simon understood suddenly that this was the honest shape of the thing. The reading would move, day to day, can to can, walk to walk, and nobody, not the WHO, not Priya, not Simon with his practiced hands, could promise a particular number on a particular Tuesday.

Friday morning Miss Okafor sat him down across a desk with a practice arm and a clipboard. Simon wrapped the cuff, listened, called the number, and then, when she asked him to interpret, he said, "It's high, and diet changes it, exercise changes it, and the WHO says less than two grams of sodium a day, less than five grams of salt, helps lower blood pressure. But it's a guideline, not a guarantee. One person can sit right under the line and still have a bad morning." Miss Okafor wrote something on her clipboard without expression. Then she set down her pen.

"That," she said, "is the answer I've been waiting three years to hear. Most of them just say 'eat less salt' like it's a punishment from God. You passed. Now go call your grandfather."

The bookshop on Miller Street had a reading group that met on Thursdays, and Charlotte had joined it under what she considered a small and forgivable pretense: she had told the owner, Mr. Petrou, that she had read Jane Eyre twice. In truth she had read it once, at fourteen, and had spent most of that reading imagining herself as Jane, which she now suspected was not the same thing at all. Tonight the group was discussing Chapter Twelve, and Charlotte had prepared by reading the chapter four times in the bath, which she felt was spiritually equivalent to a second full reading, if not better.

"You're not born wanting things," said Priya, across the circle of folding chairs. "Or maybe you are. That's the whole fight, isn't it. Does Jane want Mr. Rochester because she's Jane, or because she's a poor governess in 1847 and her options are roughly three?"

"Four," said Mr. Petrou, from behind the till, without looking up. "Governess, teacher, dependency on a relative, or death. It's a rich genre, the death option."

Charlotte had come with a plan. She wanted, very specifically, to say something that made Priya stop mid-sentence and reconsider her entire position, because Priya was a second-year philosophy student who used words like "hegemonic" at the biscuits table, and Charlotte was eighteen and about to start college and did not intend to spend the next three years being the youngest and quietest person in any room. She had a page of notes. The notes were, she admitted to herself, mostly arrows.

"Charlotte," said Priya, because silence at that table functioned as an invitation. "You've been staring at your arrow page for ten minutes."

"Margin notes," said Charlotte, closing the notebook. "A mature reader's apparatus."

She opened the book instead. There was a copy of The Second Sex on the shelf behind her chair, the orange Penguin with the cracked spine, and she had read the famous line in it twenty minutes earlier while pretending to look for the bathroom. Simone de Beauvoir, 1949. One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman. She had read it standing up between Poetry and Local Interest, feeling as though she'd shoplifted something she hadn't paid for, which technically she had, intellectually speaking.

"Here's my thing," Charlotte said. "The line from Beauvoir. The Second Sex, 1949. 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' Society shapes womanhood, Beauvoir says, it's not just installed at birth like a factory setting. So when Jane stands at the window in Chapter Twelve and says women feel restless just as men do, and need exercise for their faculties, is that her voice or is it a want she was trained to have? And if it's trained, is it less hers?" She paused. "Because I keep wanting to say trained wants are still real wants. But then the whole marriage plot looks like a contrivance, and I liked the marriage plot, Priya, I liked it at fourteen, and I refuse to be told I was fooled."

Mr. Petrou turned a page of his ledger. "Refusal is also training," he said mildly.

"Absolutely not, you don't get to do the wise bookseller thing, you did it last week." Charlotte pointed at him. "I did the reading."

"You did the reading tonight," said Priya, grinning. "In the bath, I'm guessing. Your hair's still weird on one side."

"That's a styling choice." Charlotte smoothed the flat side. "And it's not germane to Jane Eyre."

"It's completely germane to whether you titrate your convictions down to match your preparation," Priya said, "which, honestly, is kind of the method, and it's not an insult. You start strong, you add the evidence drop by drop until the color holds."

The group had gone quiet in the way it did when two people were actually getting somewhere. An older woman named Ruth, who read every nineteenth-century novel with a pencil and no mercy, leaned forward. "I'll say what nobody's said. My mother wanted the marriage plot too, and she got it, and it was a disaster, and she still re-read the endings. Wants don't have to be good for you to be real. But Beauvoir still gets her point, because where did my mother learn that the disaster ending was romantic? Not from her soul. From the shelf."

"So both," Charlotte said slowly. "Trained and real. Not one or the other."

"Or neither," said Priya, cheerfully wrecking it. "I'm not conceding."

Charlotte laughed, and Ruth took the last biscuit, and Mr. Petrou wrote something in the ledger that was probably not about books at all. On her way out, Charlotte stopped at the shelf between Poetry and Local Interest, took down the orange Penguin, and carried it to the till. She had exactly enough from her birthday. "I'm buying it now," she said, "so next week my moral superiority is fully documented." Mr. Petrou rang it up, wrapped it in yesterday's newspaper, and slid it across the counter to her, and she held it against the flat side of her hair all the way home.

The deadline was midnight, and by four in the afternoon Victoria had already broken the query twice. She sat at her grandfather's rolltop desk with her laptop open beside his old jar of fountain pens, the assignment page glowing in front of her: build two tables, customers and orders, then write a query that returns the customers who never ordered anything. The first part had gone fine. The join itself kept swallowing the very rows she wanted. Every customer with orders appeared; every customer without them vanished, as if not ordering were a kind of nonexistence.

Her grandfather was out in the riparian garden, the strip of tended green he maintained along the river's edge, cutting back the reeds before the first frost. From the window she could see his slow scissors working. He had been a typesetter before retirement, and when she'd arrived that morning he had looked over her shoulder at the screen and said the tables reminded him of ledger pages. Then he had gone back outside, leaving her alone with what he called her machinations, though what she was doing felt less like scheming than like begging a machine to admit that absence could be information.

Because that was the problem, she decided, walking her frustration out to the kitchen and back. The join matched rows to rows. A customer with no orders had no row to match, so the join dropped her, and the query reported a world in which she had never registered at all. Victoria thought of her own college applications, still half-finished on another hard drive, and of how easy it would be for some system somewhere to conclude that silence meant nobody was there.

She tried writing the condition into the WHERE clause and made it worse. She typed the table names in the wrong order, reversed them, reversed them back. In her notes she had begun to transliterate the error messages into plain English, copying "JOIN" into her notebook as if it were a foreign alphabet, sounding it out: customer LEFT OUTER JOIN order means keep all of the left table, keep the ghosts, attach whatever matches and leave the rest empty. The rest empty. She stopped with her pen down. Empty was not the same as dropped. The join could carry a row across with a hole in it, if you asked it the right way.

While she waited for the idea to settle, she texted her cousin Marcus, who had taken the course last year, and got back only a smirk emoji and "left join, null check, you'll see." Then, needing to know why the whole thing was built out of tables at all rather than something less stubborn, she searched on her phone and found her way down into the history of it. She had assumed tables were just how software happened to grow, the way her grandfather's reeds grew where they grew. Instead there was a paper. The relational model of databases was introduced by IBM researcher Edgar F. Codd in a 1970 paper, "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks." She read the title twice. Someone had invented this flat, rectangular, quietly ruthless way of holding the world, and he had worked for IBM, and it had started in 1970, in a paper with that calm, astonishing title.

"Codd," she said aloud to the empty kitchen, testing the name. It sounded like a man who would insist that everything fit somewhere.

Back at the desk she wrote it out slowly, saying the parts as if translating for her grandfather: SELECT the customer name FROM customers LEFT JOIN orders ON the matching IDs WHERE the order ID IS NULL. She ran it. The screen returned exactly three names, the three phantoms, Mrs. Okafor and two others, surfacing from the join's kept side with their empty halves showing. Not ordering, it turned out, could be stated, could be printed, could be true. Victoria sat back and looked at the three names for a long moment, honest with herself about what she still didn't understand, why the empty value behaved differently from any value she could type, and whether she could reproduce this at midnight under pressure or had merely been lucky.

At eleven forty she attached the file and pressed submit, then carried her phone out to the garden to show her grandfather the winning query, screen light against the dark river. He held it at arm's length, squinting, and read the three returned names, and then, at the top of the page, the fourth row she had missed entirely: her own name, entered in the customers table during the morning's testing, never having ordered anything. "So the system caught you," he said, handing the phone back. "You're the ghost."

The tube had been in Grandpa's shed for thirty years, sitting in a cigar box between a spool of solder and a jar of bent nails. Robert found it on the second morning of his visit, when the rain had driven him inside away from the collapsing woodpile. It was sealed glass, thumb-sized, and it held a gas the color of weak tea, though when he tilted it toward the window it looked almost brown, like the last inch of a Coke.

"Careful with that," Grandpa said from the doorway. He said it without alarm, the way he said everything, and Robert noticed he didn't come closer.

"What is it?"

"Something your uncle made before he quit caring about anything. Nitrogen dioxide, sealed up with its other form. Two gases that turn into each other and never finish." Grandpa wiped his hands on a rag that had once been a shirt. "Your grandmother wants the gutters checked. After."

Robert didn't check the gutters for an hour. He held the tube and thought about the poster board sitting in the trunk of his mother's car, the one he'd carried into the gymnasium in April with his chin up. Prediction: heating the reaction vessel increases product yield. The judges had let him run his demo in front of them. He'd warmed his flask in a water bath, watched the solution, and waited for the shift he'd promised. It had gone the wrong way. Not dramatically, not in a way anyone laughed at, but wrong, and he'd stood there and said, "That's, uh, unexpected," and the taller judge had written something down without looking up.

He texted Dana from the back step, rain ticking on the porch roof. Fixing the poster for regionals. Need the demo to work this time.

You sure it can be fixed, she wrote back. Or is the whole thing wrong?

He started to type three different answers and deleted each one. He was tired of equivocating with her, tired of the maybe-it-was-the-concentration, maybe-it-was-the-thermometer dodge he'd been running since April. He put the phone in his pocket and went back to the shed.

Grandpa's kitchen was nearly bare, plates in one cabinet, a kettle, a table with one wobble he'd shimmed with a folded hymnal insert. The house had the stripped, deliberate plainness of a man who had decided what he needed and refused the rest, and Robert had privately nicknamed it the ascetic setup, though never out loud. He filled a drinking glass with ice water and set the tube in it, and set a second tube of the same gas, which Uncle Marcus had apparently made in pairs, into a mug of water he'd boiled on the stove.

He watched. He made himself watch without hoping, which was harder than it sounded.

The cold tube faded first, its tea color thinning toward nothing, like breath fading off glass. The hot tube went the other way, deepening from weak tea to strong, a definite brown, the color of the fumes in the safety films. He swapped them, hot to cold, and the colors swapped too, slowly, like an argument that kept turning itself around. He sat with his notebook and wrote it plainly. The forward reaction makes product, and it gives off heat. When he added heat, he got less product, more reactant. The system ran backward, soaking up what he put in. When he pulled heat out, it ran forward again to replace it. He underlined nothing. He just looked at it.

"Supper's at six," Grandpa said, passing through with the rag over his shoulder. He paused at the two glasses. "Marcus called that Le Chatelier's principle. Frenchman. Said the system pushes back against whatever you do to it." He said it the way he'd say a neighbor's name, no more, and went on to the pantry.

Robert took out his phone and typed to Dana, Not fixed. Reversed. I predicted the wrong direction because I forgot the forward reaction gives off heat. New poster. Then he set the phone face down and picked up the cold tube, which was nearly colorless now, and cupped it in both hands.

The trail to Painter's Ridge began in Douglas fir shade and ended, three miles later, on a bald shoulder of granite where Luke had promised they would eat lunch by two o'clock, because the last shuttle down the mountain left the trailhead at five and Priya's mother would adjudicate all future hiking privileges based on the outcome. Priya walked behind him with a printout folded into her jacket pocket, a graph she had to understand by Monday and that Luke, having gotten a B-minus on his own attempt last spring, had claimed he could teach her.

"So explain it," Priya said, at the first switchback. "You said you'd explain it on the way up."

"Up is for warming up," Luke said. "The explanation happens at altitude."

"You're stalling."

He was stalling. The graph itself was simple enough, a line that hugged the bottom of the page until about 1950 and then climbed in a curve so smooth it looked drawn by hand, and Priya could read the numbers fine. What she could not do was say why the line mattered, and Luke's B-minus lived exactly there. He had written, on the exam, that greenhouse gases "block heat from escaping, like a lid," and his professor had circled "lid" and written "no" beside it in red, twice, which suggested a certain feeling.

They stopped where a fallen tree crossed the path and Priya held out her hand for the graph. He spread it on the trunk. The paper had been rained on once and dried wavy, a veneer of stiffness over the ink, and the sawtooth inside the curve, the little annual teeth Priya had noticed on the bus, stood up under the light like something you could feel with a thumb.

"Okay," Luke said. "The Earth's surface. It gives off heat. Not sunlight, it's the other kind, infrared."

"Heat is a type of light?"

"Radiation, yeah. Same word as the scary thing, different amount of scary." He pointed down the valley, where the clearcut patches glared pale. "All that ground down there, all day, it's been giving off infrared. Upward. Toward space."

"And it just goes?"

"It would," Luke said, and then stopped, because that was the part where his lid had lived, and he was suddenly unwilling to say it again. He thought about the rock instead, the granite they were standing on, how the slab would still be warm at nine tonight, giving off the day slowly. "No," he said. "It doesn't just go."

Priya waited. A jay came down and considered their backpacks with an expression of professional interest.

"The gases," Luke said. "Carbon dioxide, the stuff on your graph. Water vapor, some others. They absorb the infrared." He picked up a pebble and held it over the graph. "The ground sends heat up, the gas takes it in, and then it re-emits it. All directions. Up, sideways, and down. Back down at the ground."

"So the heat comes back."

"Some of it comes back. So the lower air, the part we breathe, stays warmer than it would if the infrared just left." He heard himself say it and checked it against the red double no. Nothing bounced off a lid. The gas took the heat and threw it every direction, like a crowd throwing back a beach ball, and the more gas, the more beach balls came down. He had been wrong, he realized, in a way that was almost right, which was the most annoying kind of wrong.

"The line goes up," Priya said, "because we put more of the gas in."

"Because we put a lot more in. That's the curve. Every tooth is a year, the whole thing is sixty-some years of somebody measuring it in one place, every hour, which is either dedication or a cry for help."

Priya folded the graph along its old crease. "And the teeth?"

"Seasons," Luke said. "The forest breathes." He was on thin ice here and they both knew it; he had gotten that question half wrong too, and he said so, because pretending otherwise last spring had produced a B-minus and a red no, no.

They climbed the last half mile in the open, the sun flat on the granite, and the rock gave off its stored heat against their legs through their boots. Priya kept saying it back to herself in fragments, ground, infrared, absorbed, re-emitted, all directions, down, lower atmosphere warmer, like a girl memorizing a phone number, and twice she got it wrong in new ways and Luke corrected her without, he hoped, sounding like the lid.

At the top they ate the sandwiches and looked at the haze lying over the valley like a second, man-made sky. "So what still doesn't make sense to you," Priya said, "honestly."

"Whether saying it out loud like this counts as knowing it," Luke said. "I can recite the whole thing and I still can't tell if I understand it or just believe it in a loud voice."

Priya looked at her watch and stood up. "We can be uncertain at a run," she said. "Shuttle's at five."

They ran, and the warm rock of the trail gave off its heat behind them, upward, into the crowded air.

The clip arrived at 11:40 on a Tuesday, while Liam was replacing the cracked screen of a Galaxy S9 behind the counter of his uncle's repair shop. In the video, a crowd surged around a burning van, someone shouted in a language Liam didn't recognize, and a caption in bold yellow letters claimed this was happening right now, three streets from the community college where he'd enrolled for the fall. His cousin Dara had sent it to the family group chat with the message everyone needs to see this. His thumb hovered over the forward arrow.

"Not the screen glue again," his uncle said from the back room, misreading the way Liam had gone still. The shop smelled like isopropyl alcohol and the burnt-plastic ghost of some earlier repair; a radio behind the register murmured traffic reports. Liam set the customer's phone in the foam tray and watched the clip a second time. Forty seconds. His heart was doing something he didn't like. Two kids from his graduating class had already replied to the chat with praying emoji and which street exactly.

He typed which street and then deleted it, because he realized he didn't know, and because the van in the video was parked beside a wall covered in ivy, and he could not think of a single ivy-covered wall anywhere near the college. He knew the campus. He'd walked it twice on orientation days, once in rain. There was no ivy. This was a small thing, an idiosyncrasy of the footage, and small things were what his uncle always said you checked first when a phone came in acting strange. You don't assume the motherboard. You check whether the case is pressing the power button.

Liam pulled up an image search engine on the shop's ancient tablet and tried dragging the video file into the search bar. Nothing. He tried the link, then the link plus quotation marks, then three different engines, his movements getting faster and less careful. The tablet fan whirred underpinning his frustration like a small animal. "It won't take a video," he said to the empty shop. "It just won't take a video."

The bell over the door rang, and Marisol came in with her little brother's iPhone in a sandwich bag, its screen spiderwebbed from corner to corner. Marisol had finished her first year at the state university and worked at the library, and Liam had tutored her in trig the year before, so they had that flat, pleasant history. "Is your uncle around," she started, then saw his face. "What happened?"

"Someone posted a video," Liam said. "Says there's a riot near campus. I want to check if it's real before my whole family panics, but I can't search it. The search engines won't take video."

Marisol set the sandwich bag on the counter. "You can't search a video directly," she said. "What the fact-checkers at the library do is take screenshots of key frames and search those images instead." She said it like she was handing him a screwdriver, the way you'd hand over any tool. "Pause it where something identifiable shows. A sign, a building, a face."

Liam paused the clip where the camera swung across a storefront. The frame was blurry, so he stepped back a few seconds and caught a sharper moment: a green awning, a phone number stenciled on the van's door, a distinctive arch in the background. He took a screenshot, then two more from other moments, the way you'd take multiple samples. The first screenshot returned nothing useful. The second returned a match from an image search, an article dated fourteen months earlier, from a city in another country entirely, about a truck accident during a heat wave protest. The arch was the same. The awning was the same green.

"So it's old," Liam said slowly. "It's from last year, and it's not even here."

"Or that article used an old video too," Marisol said. "That happens. One match doesn't finish it. Check the other screenshots, and look at when the earliest posts of the clip appeared."

He searched the third screenshot and found a news agency's fact-check page, which had traced the same footage to a local report from the other country, filmed during that protest. The earliest copy Liam could find on any social platform had been posted nine hours ago by an account with no history and a stock-photo profile picture. He sat back. The evidence didn't feel like a door slamming shut; it felt like four separate handrails, each one holding weight. He thought about how he'd wanted to forward it, how the wanting had felt like being helpful, urgent, part of something, and how that wanting had nothing to do with whether the video was true.

He typed into the family chat: it's from a protest in another country over a year ago, not near campus. Screenshot of the fact-check attached. Then, because Dara could get truculent when corrected in front of the aunts, he added a second message: I only knew because I got lucky with the search. Could've been me forwarding it.

Dara replied with a thumbs up and, a minute later, a private message: how did you even find that. Liam started typing an answer, stopped, and looked at the customer's half-repaired phone in its foam tray. He took a picture of the ivy frame instead and sent that, with the words: pause the video, screenshot the frame, search the image. Then he picked up the spudger, seated the new screen ribbon into its connector, and pressed the power button to watch the display bloom back to life.

The laundromat on Fairview Avenue smelled like burnt lint and lemon detergent, and Sara had claimed the plastic chair by the window because from there she could see the parking lot, where her mother's Corolla sat waiting like a patient dog. Her road test was in nine days. Between loads she went out with a rolled gym sock and practiced laying it on the passenger seat, then reaching over to check her blind spot, then pulling the sock back, because the examiner would watch her head turn and not just her eyes flick to the mirror.

Her mother's approach to driving was a single maxim, delivered the way you'd hand down a recipe: merge early, be polite. Sara had absorbed it the way she'd absorbed the recipe for scalloped potatoes, without examination, and for years it had sat in her as though it were law rather than preference. The socks tumbled in the dryer behind her now, thumping like a slow heartbeat, while she sat with her phone and read the state Department of Transportation's page on work zones, mostly to avoid thinking about the parallel parking she still couldn't do.

The construction on Highway 36 was the real problem. Her test route ran through it, and her mother insisted she get over into the open lane a half mile before the merge, which in afternoon traffic meant sitting in a queue while the closed lane stretched empty beside her, taunting. Sara had done exactly that on Tuesday, and a pickup had roared past in the empty lane, and her mother had said, "Some people," with such certainty that Sara felt disaffected from her own doubts, as if questioning the early merge were a small act of treason.

The state's page said otherwise. It said Minnesota's Department of Transportation recommends using both lanes up to the merge point and then taking turns, and it called that the zipper merge. It said the zipper merge can cut a backup's length by as much as 40 percent. Sara read the line twice, then a third time, holding the phone at an angle against the window glare. Forty percent. She had no image for what that meant in cars, so she tried to reify it, to make the abstraction solid: if the line she'd sat in on Tuesday had been ten blocks, it could have been six. Whole intersections freed up. People who would have missed a green light getting home.

A man folding towels two machines over noticed her frowning at the phone. "You look like you're doing taxes," he said. He had a gray ponytail and was folding with unusual precision, corners matched to corners.

"Driving test," Sara said. "There's construction on my route and everybody says merge early, but the state says wait and take turns at the end. They call it the zipper merge." She turned the screen toward him. "It can cut the backup by like forty percent."

"Huh," he said. "So everyone being polite is making it worse."

"I don't know if it's worse," Sara said, and realized she meant it. "It feels worse to wait. You feel like a cheat driving down the empty lane. But it's not cheating if everyone's supposed to do it."

Her mother arrived at four to help fold, and Sara raised it on the drive home, carefully, the way you'd test a frozen lake. Her mother's jaw set. "If everybody merged early there'd be no problem at all."

"There'd still be a backup," Sara said. "Just a longer one." She didn't push further. Her mother had driven thirty years without a single accident, and Sara was seventeen with a gym sock standing in for a passenger, and it occurred to her that experience and information were two different currencies, and she wasn't sure which one the road took.

They practiced parallel parking in the church lot on Spruce Street, between her mother's car and a row of battered orange cones Sara had borrowed from the community center. First attempt, she clipped a cone and sent it rolling like a severed head. "That cone had a family," her mother said, deadpan, and Sara laughed so hard she had to put the car in park. Second attempt she over-corrected and ended up facing the cones at a diagonal, close to the curb but philosophically confused. Third attempt, hands at ten and two, reversing until the cone vanished from the rear window, one full turn of the wheel, back until the front cone lined up with her shoulder, the other way, and the Corolla slid into the space with a foot to spare on either side. Her mother said nothing, which was her highest praise.

Saturday they drove the test route, and when the orange signs appeared on Highway 36, Sara stayed in the closing lane. Her mother's hand tightened on the armrest. Cars passed them in the right lane, slow and orderly, and at the merge point a hatchback flashed its lights and let her in, one car, one at a time, like teeth closing. Sara lifted two fingers off the wheel in thanks. Behind her the line of cars kept alternating, and ahead the backup was shorter than she'd ever seen it, though she couldn't say how much, and her mother said, quietly, almost to herself, "Well," and then said nothing else the rest of the way to the exit.

Amelia had signed the card at the language booth mostly to get the free cloth bookmark, and only afterward understood what she had agreed to: five minutes, on the stage under the paper lanterns, debating whether the city should cut its arts budget to fund housing, entirely in Mandarin. She had studied for three years, but three years of classroom sentence drills had not prepared her for a microphone and an audience eating skewered squid twenty feet away.

She found her assigned partner behind the tea stand, a boy named Deshawn from the bilingual school across town, who was fanning himself with the debate topic sheet. "You're the one who signed up late," he said. "Good. You can take the opening. I'll do rebuttal." He made it sound like a mercy, though she suspected it was strategy: an unprepared partner spends her minutes collapsing while he sweeps in at the end.

They had forty minutes to prepare. Amelia argued, in her careful textbook Chinese, that housing came first, that a person needs walls before she needs murals. Deshawn pushed back in quick, loose Mandarin she could barely follow, and when she asked him to slow down he switched to English without seeming to notice, then back again, sometimes in the same sentence, the way her aunt did on the phone. "You keep doing that," Amelia said.

"Doing what?"

"Going between the two. Mid-sentence."

He shrugged, still fanning himself. "That's just code-switching. Everybody fluent does it. It doesn't mean your Chinese is bad." She wanted to believe him, because in the last ten minutes she had caught herself doing it too, English words surfacing whenever the Mandarin ran thin, like reflexes her mouth reached for on its own. She wrote her notes in characters anyway, all of them, refusing herself the escape hatch, and told herself the discipline would hold.

It did not entirely hold. On stage, under lights strung between two poles, she got through her first argument cleanly, and then a man in the second row raised his hand for the cross-examination period and asked something about property taxes that dismantled her vocabulary. She heard herself say "the revenue, I mean the money, the revenue," and a ripple of laughter went through the crowd, kind or otherwise she could not tell. Her face went hot. The moderator, an older woman in a silk jacket, leaned toward the microphone and said, kindly but audibly, "English words will not count toward your five minutes."

Afterward Amelia sat on the curb by the food stalls, working through a paper boat of rice the way other people worked through a problem, methodically, without pleasure. Deshawn found her there. "You lost the thread in cross-ex," he said, sitting down without being invited. "But your opening was better than mine would've been. The walls-before-murals thing. That was good."

"It fell apart."

"It switched. It's not the same as falling apart." He tore the top off her boat and stole some rice, and she let him, because it seemed like the price of the conversation. "My grandmother does it constantly. She'll say half a sentence in Cantonese and finish it in English and no one in my house thinks she's stupid. But the moderator's right too. Under the rules, only one language counts. So you practice holding one track for five minutes. That's a different skill."

Amelia turned that over while a group of dancers in embroidered jackets noisily assembled near the stage, their drums already rumbling under the announcement for the next act. Two things could both be true, she decided: that her slipping was not evidence of failure, and that the rules of this particular stage demanded a fluency she did not have yet, a single-rail fluency that would atrophy, she suspected, if she avoided the English crutch for a year and then lost her nerve and never went back up. Her position on the arts budget had wobbled too, somewhere between Deshawn's argument that a festival like this one was proof the arts fed people in their own way and her own stubborn insistence on walls. She had ended her rebuttal, haltingly, by conceding that both mattered and proposing a split no council would ever adopt, and she could not tell whether that was wisdom or cowardice.

"Next one's in October," Deshawn said, standing, brushing rice off his jeans. "The school tournament. You'd be my actual partner, not a walk-in." The drums started in earnest, and behind him the aesthete running the calligraphy booth was arguing with a volunteer about whether the lanterns hung at the right height, both of them gesturing up into the dusk. Amelia looked at the stage, then at the sign-up table, where the woman in the silk jacket was already pinning up a fresh sheet for the next debate. "Save me a slot," she said, and got up before she could think better of it.

Vanessa had promised her mother she would come to the bank on Saturday, and the promise was the reason she was still in the economics classroom at four o'clock, rewriting an index card she had already rewritten twice. Her mother wanted to compare mortgage offers and had said, half joking, that Vanessa was the one in the family taking economics. That was in September. Since then the assignment had landed on the class like weather: each student had to stand up on Friday and explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation, in plain words, for a hypothetical listener who knew nothing.

The hypothetical listener was the problem. Vanessa could recite the chain in her sleep. Higher rates make borrowing more expensive, so households buy fewer houses and cars, so demand falls, so prices stop climbing so fast. But reciting was not explaining, and she knew the difference because of what had happened to Priya last week. Priya had stood at the whiteboard and delivered a flawless paragraph, and Mr. Okafor had said only, "Now say it to your grandmother," and Priya had gone blank. Vanessa did not want to go blank in front of thirty people. More than that, she did not want to go blank at the bank, in front of her mother and a loan officer with a tie, on the biggest purchase her family had ever considered.

She tried it out on Luis, who sat across from her dismantling a pen. "Rates today are so different from a few years ago," she began. "Why?" Luis expostulated, waving the pen spring at her, "That's what I keep asking my parents. They refinanced when money was basically free and now they act like I personally set the rates." Vanessa laughed, then stopped laughing, because the numbers were sitting in her notes and she had not yet made them speak. She copied them onto the fresh card in her smallest, most careful hand: the Federal Reserve began raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it had reached a range of 5.25 to 5.50 percent. That was not a mechanism. That was history. But history was what her mother would be holding in her hand on Saturday, a printed offer sheet with a rate that would have looked impossible three years earlier.

Friday came. Vanessa was third, after a boy who mumbled about "cooling the economy" as though it were soup. She stood, and she did not look at Mr. Okafor. She looked at the back wall and pretended it was the bank lobby, vinyl chairs, her mother's good coat.

"Pretend I'm at the bank with my mom," she said. "She's looking at mortgage offers and she asks why the rates are so different from a few years ago. So I'd tell her the Fed started raising its policy rate from near zero in March 2022, and by July 2023 it was between 5.25 and 5.50 percent. Then she'd ask what that has to do with a mortgage. And I'd say the Fed's rate is the price of money itself. When money gets expensive, everything bought with borrowed money gets expensive too. People take out fewer loans. They buy less. When buyers pull back, sellers can't keep pushing prices up, and inflation slows. It's like the Fed turning down the temperature in a house where everyone has been fighting over the thermostat."

She heard herself say it and it sounded simple, which frightened her, because simple things were the ones she usually got wrong. Mr. Okafor asked one question: where does it hurt? She said, "Borrowers first. Anyone renewing, anyone starting out. It slows the whole economy on purpose, and the Fed decides how much pain is worth it." He nodded once and wrote something, and she sat down before her knees could change their minds.

That was the classroom, and it went well, and it is where Vanessa's part of this story would like to end. But at the back of the room, in the chair reserved for the teacher who was observing that period, sat Ms. Adeyemi from the counseling office, and she had not come to grade economics.

She had come because of a phone call. Vanessa's mother had called the school on Wednesday, quiet and hurried, asking whether students could access copies of their transcripts before the semester ended. Ms. Adeyemi had recognized the surname, had pulled the file, and had seen what Vanessa did not know anyone had seen: the withdrawal from the private college with the early scholarship, logged in August, and then nothing. A gap year, the file said, in the mother's handwriting on a form. Ms. Adeyemi suspected, from the sound of the phone call and the mortgage question underneath it, that the gap year was a polite word for something else. She watched the girl explain interest rates with an incisiveness that made the other students sit still, watched her say it's like turning down the temperature, and thought: this one has already taught herself the cost of borrowed money in a way no class covers.

When the bell rang, Ms. Adeyemi caught her in the hallway, near the trophy case. "Your presentation," she said. "Are you giving it anywhere else?" Vanessa said, "The bank. Saturday. My mom's refinancing." She said it lightly, the way you hand someone a fact that is not the whole fact. Ms. Adeyemi did not offer the bromide about doors opening and closing, though it rose to her mouth. Instead she said, "If you ever want to talk about next year, my door's open."

Vanessa said thank you and walked on, card in her pocket, numbers still legible under her thumb where she had pressed too hard with the pen. At the corner of the corridor she stopped, took out her phone, and texted her mother: still good for Saturday? bring the offers from three years ago too. She stood looking at the screen until the three dots appeared.

The shop sat between a dry cleaner and a shuttered nail salon, and Mackenzie had worked the front counter for six weeks, taking in phones with cracked screens and logging each one into the database her boss's nephew had built two summers ago. The nephew had gone off to a bootcamp and stopped answering emails, so when the owner, Deshawn, needed to know which customers had never picked up an order, the question landed on her.

"You took a class," Deshawn said. He said it the way he said most things, flat, as if stating a price. "One semester of computers. That's more than me."

One semester, and most of it spreadsheet work. But the shop's system ran on something called SQL, and she had a phone open under the counter to a tutorial site, and a query that almost worked. There was a table of customers and a table of orders. She wanted the customers who appeared in the first table and not in the second. The tutorial called this finding missing matches. She wrote it on Tuesday night at the little desk in her room, the screen light falling through the diaphanous curtain her mother had hung instead of blinds, and the query returned four names. She printed them on the shop's ancient receipt printer, because Deshawn trusted paper.

On Thursday he called from the back room, where he was trying to suture a ribbon cable back onto a water-damaged logic board, his term for it, held with Kapton tape and patience. "Mackenzie. It's wrong. I called two of these people and they've got orders in the system. Sitting right there."

She came back and looked. He was right. One of the four names belonged to a woman with a pending screen replacement, order number in the orders table, plain as anything. Her query had said the woman ordered nothing. She stood there while a customer at the counter waited to pay twelve dollars for a charger, and after she rang him up she pulled the query up again and stared at it.

She ran it in pieces. She ran the inner part alone, the list of customer IDs from the orders table, and counted the rows. Then she compared it to what she expected, and found one more row than there should have been. The last row said NULL. Someone, at some point, had saved an order with the customer field left blank. She remembered the day, actually: a Saturday rush, a walk-in who wouldn't give his name, Deshawn saying just put it in, we'll fix the record later. Nobody had fixed the record.

She deleted the NULL row the honest way first, finding the blank order and attaching a name to it, a walk-in named R. Osei who had paid cash. Then she reran her query. The list came back different, shorter, correct as far as she could verify by hand. She reran the original query with the blank still in place, on a copy of the data, and got nothing. Not four wrong names. Nothing at all, zero rows, where before there had been four. The blank had swallowed the whole result.

She sat with that for a while, because it did not seem like something a list should be able to do. One empty value, and the question stopped being answered at all. She thought of her mother's church, the one her aunt ran like a small theocracy, where a single doubt in the room could end the whole evening's testimony. She didn't like that she thought of it, and she didn't entirely trust the comparison, but it stayed in her head anyway.

"Deshawn," she called to the back. "Come look at this." She showed him the two runs, side by side. "A NOT IN subquery returns no rows at all if the list has even one NULL," she said. "That's the trap. That's what it's called in the docs, a trap. Somebody saved an order with a blank customer, and the whole query came back empty."

He leaned on the counter and read both screens twice. "So the list was broken before, with the four names, and broken after, with none."

"Right. Both wrong, in different directions."

"So which is it now?"

"Now it's right, but only because I fixed the blank by hand. If another one gets saved, it breaks again. I don't know how to stop that yet." She pulled the receipt printer closer and tore off the fresh list, four names that checked out, two of them people she recognized. "You could call these two today. The other two I'd email."

He folded the paper into his shirt pocket and went back to the ribbon cable. Mackenzie opened a new tab next to the tutorial, one with the database's own documentation in it, and started typing.

The trail behind the reservoir climbed in short switchbacks, and Victoria stopped at the second bend because her brother had promised to quiz her there, at the flat rock shaped like a dinner plate. Theo was twenty and impecunious in the way college students were, which was why he tutored her for free instead of the twelve dollars an hour the student center charged, and why the quizzing happened outdoors, where nobody had to buy anything. She spread her notebook on the rock and uncapped a marker. "Draw me a cell," he said. "Just the outline. Then tell me where everything goes."

She drew a lopsided circle and began filling it: a nucleus like a plum, then a scattering of kidney beans for mitochondria. He crouched beside her and pointed at the beans. "Start there. Glucose comes in, what happens?" She bent over the diagram, tongue between her teeth, and wrote GLYCOLYSIS with an arrow pointing straight into the nearest bean, because the whole unit was called cellular respiration and the mitochondria were the power plants, and where else would a power plant take its fuel. Theo didn't say anything, which was worse than saying something.

She thought back to Tuesday, to the classroom with its smell of disinfectant and the quiz she had failed, the one that had started all this. Ms. Okafor had asked her at the board where the process began and she had stood with the chalk hovering over her drawing of a mitochondrion, and the hovering had gone on so long that a boy in the second row laughed, and she had written the arrow anyway, into the bean, into the wrongness. That was the day she decided she would learn it so thoroughly that hovering would never happen again. It was also the day she began to suspect that biology might be less like a diagram and more like a trail, where a path branched before you expected it to.

"Say it out loud," Theo said now, tapping the rock. "Use the diagram." She pointed at her arrow and recited what she'd memorized from the textbook, and when she finished he shook his head slowly. "The quizlet has it. Look." He held out his phone, and she read the screen twice, then a third time, because the sentence refused to fit into her drawing. Glycolysis happens in the cytoplasm, outside the mitochondria, and splits one glucose molecule into two pyruvate molecules for a net gain of two ATP. The fuel didn't enter the power plant first. It was broken in half on the doorstep, in the open soup of the cell, and only the pieces went inside.

"Outside," she said. "The first step is outside." She crossed out her arrow with the marker until the rock went gray, then drew a new one that stopped short of the bean, in the empty space she had thought of as nothing. That nothing was the cytoplasm. That nothing was where everything started. "One glucose in, two pyruvate out," she said, sketching the two smaller shapes like a split river around a stone, "and you get two ATP for it. Net. Only two, even though it feels like it should be more." Theo nodded and folded the phone away.

He watched her redraw the whole diagram from memory, and from where he stood the marker looked like a small walking stick in her fist. She had always wanted certainty from him, wanted him to contextualize each fact inside some larger order so that memorizing felt like discovering rather than copying, and he had never been able to give her that, because the order kept revising itself in his own lectures and textbooks.
